scope: These are species annotations, not confirmed strains. A gut resident normally lives in the intestine; that does not make it always useful or harmless. Some can cause infection outside the gut. Stool abundance alone does not identify harmful traits or prove a health benefit.

entries.name: Bacteroides uniformis
entries.usualRole: Gut resident; specific strains have shown potential benefits. Strain CECT 7771 improved metabolic and some immune measures in obese mice.
entries.caution: Those animal results do not establish a benefit from Sid’s unidentified strains, or make a lower share harmful.

entries.name: Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron
entries.usualRole: Gut resident that helps break down complex carbohydrates. It has also been studied in CTLA-4 cancer immunotherapy.
entries.caution: It can cause infections outside the gut. The immunotherapy findings do not establish that this increase benefits Sid or prevents recurrence.

entries.name: Bacteroides finegoldii
entries.usualRole: Gut resident; what its change means for Sid’s health is uncertain.
entries.caution: A case report found bloodstream infection in a person with major bowel disease. Finding it in stool is not evidence of that infection.

entries.name: Bacteroides cellulosilyticus
entries.usualRole: Gut resident that can break down many complex carbohydrates in food.
entries.caution: The cited work studied strain WH2 in laboratory and mouse models; a useful digestive function does not make abundance a health target.

entries.name: Bacteroides xylanisolvens
entries.usualRole: Gut resident that breaks down xylan, a type of plant fiber.
entries.caution: One particular strain, DSM 23964, passed specific safety studies. These profiles do not identify that strain or establish a treatment benefit.
